name: Drogheda
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Drogheda | Coasters on the Boyne
description: Thickness measurement for coasters, small bulk carriers and general cargo ships at Drogheda Port on the River Boyne: holds, tanks and piping on cargo stops.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at Drogheda Port and Tom Roe's Point
intro: Drogheda Port lies on the tidal River Boyne in County Louth, north of Dublin on Ireland's east coast. It is a port for coasters and small bulk and general cargo ships, handling animal feed and grain, fertiliser, break-bulk, LPG and exports of waste-derived fuel at the Tom Roe's Point terminal and the town quays. The ships are small but busy, and many return on regular short-sea rotations. Our technicians fly in from India for each job and gauge holds, tanks and piping while the cargo is worked.

highlights.p: Coasters on short-sea feed, fertiliser and break-bulk trades call at Drogheda again and again. A gauging scope can be divided across visits, which suits owners who want to track wastage on a ship they intend to keep trading rather than measure everything in one go.

At the town quays, ships sit on soft, level mud at low water. That ties arrivals and departures to the tide and gives a predictable, steady working period alongside, in which holds and tanks can be opened, ventilated and gauged without the ship moving.

Exports of solid recovered fuel and refuse-derived fuel, and an LPG terminal on the river, bring ships with their own inspection needs: hold condition on bulk ships loading waste-derived fuel, and deck and cargo piping on small gas carriers.

port.h: Drogheda: a tidal river port on the Boyne
p: Drogheda stands a short way up the River Boyne from its mouth between Mornington and Baltray, on the boundary of counties Louth and Meath. Ships cross the bar at the river mouth and follow a channel held in place by training walls up the estuary, so the port works to the tide: laden ships arrive and leave around high water, and the river's limits on length and draught keep the traffic to coasters and small bulk and general cargo vessels. Upstream, the Boyne Viaduct carries the Dublin to Belfast railway high over the river and sets an air-draught limit for the berths beyond it. Drogheda Port Company runs the harbour, with its deep-water terminal at Tom Roe's Point and the older town quays on the north bank, west of the viaduct.

The port's business is mainly agricultural and industrial bulk and break-bulk. Animal feed and grain come in for the farms of the north-east and are held in the port's bonded warehouses; fertiliser and general break-bulk are regular imports; and the port has a facility for exporting solid recovered fuel and refuse-derived fuel made from waste. An LPG terminal and the jetty serving the Premier Periclase magnesia works add specialised traffic, while project and outsized cargo uses the open storage areas. Most of the ships are coasters and small multipurpose vessels trading with Britain and the near Continent, often on rotations that bring the same hull back every few weeks. Plans for a deep-water port on the coast south of Drogheda have been discussed for years, but today's traffic is set by what the Boyne can take.

Inspection windows at Drogheda come from the tide and the cargo. A coaster arriving on one tide often leaves on a later one, and at the town quays she spends the low water sitting on the mud, alongside and motionless, which is a good time to work in holds and tanks. Discharging feed or loading waste-derived fuel takes the better part of a day for many of these ships, enough to gauge a hold or two, the hatch covers and a selection of ballast tanks. There is no drydock on the Boyne; the yards that dock coasters are in Britain, the Netherlands and elsewhere on the Continent, so Drogheda gauging is usually the advance work that tells an owner what the next docking will involve. Strong onshore winds can make the bar difficult and delay arrivals, and the plan allows for it.

facilities.h: Where coasters are gauged at Drogheda
p: Tom Roe's Point is the deep-water terminal and takes the larger ships calling at Drogheda, with room for them to swing in the river. Bulk cargo here is handled by mobile material handlers, and gauging follows them: a hold is measured once it has been emptied and swept, and tank entry is arranged with the crew under the ship's permit system. The LPG terminal and the Premier Periclase jetty operate under their own site rules, so work on ships berthed there is limited to what each terminal allows while cargo is transferring.

At the town quays the ships rest on soft mud at low water, which keeps them still and makes internal work straightforward, although trim and list change as the tide leaves the hull and that affects ventilation and access in some tanks. Upper-deck items, hatch covers and coamings, air pipes and engine-room piping can all be reached during a normal call. The external bottom shell and sea chests cannot be measured without a docking, and launch work at an anchorage is rarely practical for ships of this size, which only wait off the bar briefly for the tide.
list: Tom Roe's Point terminal — hold, tank and hatch cover gauging on the larger bulk and general cargo ships calling at Drogheda.
Town quays west of the Boyne Viaduct — internal gauging on coasters lying on the mud over low water.
LPG terminal — deck and cargo piping UT on small gas carriers within the terminal's rules.
Premier Periclase jetty — deck and hold readings on ships serving the magnesia works, as the site permits.
Waste-derived fuel loading — hold plating and coating checks on bulk ships before and after loading.

context.h: EU rules and port state control for ships at Drogheda
p: As an Irish port, Drogheda falls under EU maritime law, and port state control is the responsibility of the Marine Survey Office within the Department of Transport, working under the Paris MoU. Small, older coasters on short-sea trades are a familiar target for PSC across north-west Europe, and the deficiencies recorded on them often concern hatch covers, hold structure, ballast tanks and deck fittings such as air pipes. Current thickness readings, together with evidence of planned steel renewal, help a master show an inspector that wastage visible on board is known and being managed.

Since the end of 2020, ships under the flag of a non-EU state have needed an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board to call at an EU port, and that includes coasters under non-EU flags arriving at Drogheda. Ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above also carry EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime obligations, although many of the smallest coasters on the Boyne fall below that threshold. In the waste-derived fuel trade the cargo is governed by the EU's waste shipment rules, and owners loading it want holds in a condition where the cargo will not damage the structure or contaminate the next cargo carried.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Drogheda
jobs.p: Drogheda jobs are small in scale but frequent. Owners of coasters on regular Boyne calls use them to track hold and ballast tank wastage between dockings, to prepare steel estimates before an intermediate or renewal survey, and to check a ship's condition before buying or chartering her. Because each call is short and tide-bound, we agree with the superintendent exactly which tanks will be gas-freed and ventilated, which holds will be clean, and in what order, so the team spends its time measuring rather than waiting. Readings are delivered in class TM formats so they can be passed straight to the docking yard.
list: Hold and double bottom gauging on a coaster lying on the mud at the town quays, ahead of an intermediate survey.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of a small general cargo ship during a feed discharge at Tom Roe's Point.
Hatch cover and coaming readings on a break-bulk carrier after leaks were reported on the voyage.
Deck and cargo piping UT on a small LPG carrier at the river terminal.
Ballast tank gauging spread over three or four regular calls by the same coaster.

logistics: Dublin Airport is the arrival point for Drogheda, which lies to its north along the M1 motorway, and the town also has a station on the Dublin to Belfast railway. Ireland runs its own visa system outside the Schengen area, so the team travels from India on Irish visas, applied for once the ship's call is confirmed; a trip that continues to Warrenpoint or Belfast needs UK permission too. Access to the town quays and the terminal at Tom Roe's Point is arranged through the ship's agent and the port company.

faqs.q: Can ships be gauged while sitting on the mud at Drogheda's town quays?
faqs.a: Yes, and low water is often the steadiest time to work. The ship is alongside and resting on soft mud, so holds, tanks and the engine room can be gauged without any movement. The crew should allow for the list and trim changing as she settles, which affects tank ventilation and access, and we plan enclosed-space entry around that with the chief officer.

faqs.q: How big a scope fits into a Drogheda call?
faqs.a: For a typical coaster spending a tide or two alongside, a realistic scope is one or two holds, the hatch covers and coamings, several ballast tanks and selected engine-room piping, provided the crew has the tanks ventilated before arrival. Larger scopes are split across calls, and because many ships return on regular rotations, that rarely delays the result by much.

faqs.q: Where do coasters trading to Drogheda go for drydocking?
faqs.a: There is no drydock on the Boyne, and the yards that dock small cargo ships are in Britain, the Netherlands and other continental countries. Gauging at Drogheda beforehand gives the superintendent a steel estimate to send to the yard, which helps it plan plate and staging and shortens the time the ship has to spend in the dock.

faqs.q: Do you inspect holds used for waste-derived fuel?
faqs.a: Yes. Solid recovered fuel and refuse-derived fuel can be damp and can leave residues, so the hold steel and its coating deserve checking. We gauge hold plating and frames, note coating breakdown and pitting, and report areas that need attention before the ship returns to other cargoes. The work is done once the hold has been discharged and cleaned.
